source.title: Gradient descent reaches arbitrary accuracy in a fixed number of large steps on multiclass logistic regression

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study proves results about gradient descent reaching low loss and a perfect training classifier, but on convex multiclass logistic regression rather than the non-convex networks or settings in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study tests full-batch gradient descent on separable multiclass logistic regression. Its neural-network references are cited prior work, not this study's results. The logistic-regression findings do not measure any listed version's network behavior.
record.test_reason: The study proves large-step convergence results for separable linear logistic regression, a related optimization setting outside every listed version. It does not test neural-network training, curvature approaching a stability threshold, or divergence above that threshold. Neural-network findings appear as prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors additionally establish multiclass two-phase convergence and an O(1/T²) last-iterate loss guarantee. Their counterexample also establishes the order-sharp necessity of score-gap dependence for reaching stability or prescribed loss by the perceptron termination time.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes full-batch gradient descent on convex multiclass logistic regression from zero initialization, rather than training non-convex neural networks on image benchmarks.
record.method_sensitivity: The step-size threshold depends on the dataset through the positive score gap δ; the counterexample shows transition time cannot be bounded uniformly using only n and γ in dimension three.

fits_no_version.finding: For each fixed separable multiclass dataset, sufficiently large constant-step GD from zero reaches arbitrary cross-entropy accuracy at the hard perceptron's termination time, bounded by floor(4n/γ²) + 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Separable multiclass logistic regression admits arbitrary loss accuracy within a fixed, data-dependent iteration count by increasing the constant step size.

fits_no_version.finding: For any prescribed iteration count, sufficiently large step sizes admit a three-point separable binary dataset whose GD trajectory remains outside the stable region beyond that count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Uniform large-step transition guarantees for separable logistic regression in dimension three require dataset information beyond sample count and margin.

record.problems: The main results are theoretical guarantees for separable logistic regression, not experimental results on non-convex networks or benchmark training error. The counterexample is a constructed dataset family and establishes failure of a uniform bound for that construction.

untested.parts: All parts: convolutional-network training error on CIFAR, label corruption, model size, stopping and regularization.
All parts: ReLU teacher-student local minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
All parts: depth degradation, identity shortcuts and special initialization in plain or residual networks.
All parts: activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonality, training speed and trainable depth.
All parts: squared-loss wide-network recovery, curvature reduction, sharpness at the stability threshold and divergence conditions.
All parts: batch normalization's effects on accuracy gains and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Theoretical results can test claims, but these results concern a different model class and loss. Their resemblance to V5 does not justify linking them to it.

versions.untested_parts: Convolutional networks, CIFAR datasets, corrupted or random labels, and the effects of model size, early stopping, or regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Network depth, normalization, identity shortcuts, and training error in plain or residual networks.
Activation-specific initialization, signal propagation, orthogonal or Gaussian initialization, and trainable network depth.
Wide networks with squared loss, stability thresholds, sharpness, and divergence behavior.
Batch normalization, training speed and learning-rate tolerance in neural networks, and Fixup.

rows.subject: multiclass logistic regression
rows.size_stated: n data points in d dimensions with K ≥ 2 classes; n, d, and K are dataset-dependent
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent from W(0) = 0 with constant step size; for any ε ∈ (0, 1), a data-dependent step-size threshold gives loss below ε at a fixed iteration T.

conditions.value: linearly separable; ||xi|| ≤ 1 and positive margin γ
at least the data-dependent threshold η*ε in Theorem 5.1
T is the hard-perceptron termination time, with T ≤ floor(4n/γ²) + 1

rows.value: f(W(T)) < ε for any ε ∈ (0, 1), under the stated step-size condition
rows.note: The theorem is a guarantee for each fixed separable dataset; it does not report a benchmark experiment or training classification-error rate.
rows.check: The loss guarantee is accurately recorded, but concerns linear logistic regression rather than any version's neural networks. Its state cannot establish a listed effect.

rows.subject: multiclass hard perceptron (HP)
rows.size_stated: n data points in d dimensions with K ≥ 2 classes; n, d, and K are dataset-dependent
rows.operation_detail: Hard-perceptron dynamics from Z̃(0) = 0 reach a perfect classifier and terminate.
rows.measure: Training classification: every training example is strictly classified correctly
rows.value: Reaches a perfect classifier within T ≤ floor(4n/γ²) + 1 iterations
rows.note: This is the limiting hard-perceptron dynamics used to analyze gradient descent; it is not a neural network.
rows.check: The perfect-classifier guarantee is accurately recorded for the limiting hard perceptron. It is an auxiliary theoretical result outside all listed versions.

rows.subject: binary logistic regression on dataset Xη
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent from zero with a step size η; the constructed dataset depends on η.

conditions.value: linearly separable; three points, each of norm at most 1, with margin at least 1/(2√13)
for every N ≥ 1, sufficiently large η

rows.measure: Iterations to enter the stable region, defined in the paper by fbin(w) < 1/η
rows.value: Requires more than N iterations to enter the stable region
rows.note: This counterexample challenges a uniform transition-time guarantee for the stated family of convex logistic-regression datasets; it is not evidence about the listed neural-network versions.
rows.check: The counterexample is accurately recorded in binary conventions, but 'absent' cannot describe a listed effect here. Delayed entry into a loss sublevel on datasets depending on the step size establishes neither divergence nor failure of neural-network recovery.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
